newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO wrangle poses post-enlargement puzzle. [CORRECTED 13:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: NATO wrangle poses post-enlargement puzzle. [CORRECTED 13:30 GMT]

text.p: A transatlantic wrangle over how many former communist European countries to invite to join NATO at a summit in Madrid next week has thrown the spotlight on what enlargement means for the security of the rest of Europe.

Supporters of enlargement argue that even a limited expansion bringing in Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary will eliminate forever the division created by the Cold War and spread Western Europe's zone of stability further eastwards.

"The strongest argument in favour is that not to have done so would have sent a message that eastern and central Europe should be left in some form of suspended animation," said Jonathan Eyal of London's Royal United Services Institute.
But critics say countries likely to be excluded are those that most need to come under the West's protective shield.

Romania and Bulgaria border the Black Sea -- a currently highly fragile area of immense potential wealth and strategic importance -- while Slovenia borders the Balkans and the Baltic states remain wary of a resurgence of a nationalist Russia.

A growing band of sceptics argue an enlargement limited to three essentially stable countries simply pushes the dividing line in Europe further east, leaving the countries left out in a security vacuum which the Europeans cannot fill.
Supporters reject those arguments, saying Madrid simply marks the start of a continuing process.

"The goal here is transatlantic stability... we want to enter a period of European history when the emphasis is on inclusion and not exclusion," U.S. Senator Joseph Lieberman (corrects name) told reporters on Wednesday.

Lieberman, a member of a high-level Senate team visiting NATO's headquarters, said he believed the Senate would ratify enlargement, but warned the debate in the U.S. was just starting and would be "spirited and demanding".

France and Germany are leading a campaign to widen the expansion to include Slovenia and Romania, while the United States has said it wants the first wave restricted to the leading three and says there is no question of a compromise.
The stand-off, which comes at a time of renewed U.S. frustration at Europe's failure to play a greater role in its own defence, is unlikely to be resolved until the eve of the July 8-9 Madrid summit.

Independent analysts concede there is no question of more than three countries now being invited to join the alliance, but say the Europeans are holding out for firm commitments on future rounds of enlargement.
"All NATO countries insist on an 'open door', but what that exactly means is what is now being debated," said one alliance official.

Some countries would like NATO to pledge to invite in more members from former communist Europe at its 50th anniversary in 1999 when Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic formally join at the end of a two-year ratification process.
Others, particularly from the southern bloc of NATO countries, want a commitment that future enlargements will preserve the geographical balance between north and south.

Underlying the arguments are deep suspicions that the U.S. administration will drop enlargement after it has paid what are seen as historic debts to Poland and the Czech republic, first abandoned by the West to Nazi Germany then the Soviet Union.

Analysts say President Bill Clinton, who has seen NATO enlargement as the main foreign policy achievement of his second term, will have departed the field and question whether successors will have the stomach for a new row with Russia.

In May, this year the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) effectively bought off Russian hostility to its former satellites joining the alliance by agreeing a new cooperative relationship known as the NATO-Russia Council.
Moscow, however, has made it clear it sees enlargement as a strictly limited process.
Analysts say Germany, NATO's largest European member and a strong advocate of enlargement, could also lose interest despite its current soothing words in support of Romania's admittance.
"For the first time in its history, Germany will be surrounded by friendly states. Will it then be in its security interests to support more enlargement?" Eyal said.
